input:
In this example, we will work through the calculation of the log-mean temperature difference for a countercurrent heat exchanger that cools a process stream from 200 °C to 150 °C, using cooling water that enters at 40 °C and leaves at 65 °C.

We establish the terminal temperature differences at the two ends of the exchanger. At the end where the process stream enters, the terminal difference, denoted $\Delta T_1$, is 135 K, reflecting the difference between the entering process stream at 200 °C and the leaving water at 65 °C. At the other end, where the process stream leaves, the terminal difference $\Delta T_2$ is 110 K, reflecting the difference between the leaving process stream at 150 °C and the entering water at 40 °C. In this case the process stream undergoes the larger temperature change of the two streams, and the terminal differences are correspondingly further apart than the closest approach occurring anywhere within the unit.

$$\Delta T_{lm} = \frac{\Delta T_1 - \Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1 / \Delta T_2)}$$

In this relation, $\Delta T_{lm}$ denotes the log-mean temperature difference, while $\Delta T_1$ and $\Delta T_2$ denote the terminal differences at the two ends of the exchanger. Substituting the terminal differences into the relation gives $\Delta T_{lm}$ = 122.1 K. It is worth noting that simply taking the arithmetic mean of the two terminal differences would overstate the driving force, since the local temperature difference does not vary in a linear fashion along the exchanger; the log-mean value weights the smaller differences in the correct manner. In practice, heat-exchanger rating uses the log-mean temperature difference as the mean driving force for the unit as a whole.

It should be emphasised that the log-mean temperature difference is valid for an exchanger in which the overall coefficient remains constant along the length and neither stream undergoes a phase change. If either stream changes phase, or if the coefficient varies with temperature, the calculation moves outside the conditions under which the relation holds, and the exchanger must instead be rated in sections, with each section having its own log-mean difference. Finally, the value of 122.1 K lies between the terminal differences of 135 K and 110 K, and somewhat nearer to the smaller of the two, exactly as a logarithmic mean of the end values must.
